processing: Finished green tea, usually a local baked base, is scented with fresh zhulan flowers (Chloranthus spicatus). The rule is same-day flowers, same-day scenting: blossoms are picked in the early morning and laid in with the tea that day.
harvest_season: The base tea is a spring green; the flowers are picked in the early mornings from April to August, so scenting follows the bloom.
appearance_dry: Dark green strands, typical of a baked green base, sometimes with tiny yellow flower beads mixed in.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale yellow-green, typical of a scented green.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf, typical of a baked green base, with any flower remains spent and pale.
taste_profile: A soft green tea carrying the sweet perfume of the flower. Little is documented about this tea's taste across steeps, so expect it to behave like other scented greens, with the scent strongest early on.

brewing.notes: As with other scented greens, use a lidded gaiwan or mug to keep the aroma in, and water below the boil so the base does not turn harsh.

vintage_note: Usually sold in the year it is scented, and at its best within about a year while the perfume is fresh, as is normal for scented greens. It is not an ageing tea. Ask which base tea was used, since Shexian makers scent grades from everyday baked green up to named local greens.
description:
Zhulan Huacha is a green tea scented with zhulan, the tiny yellow flowers of Chloranthus spicatus, and Shexian in southern Anhui is the place that has made it a local identity. It sits in the same family as jasmine tea, but the flower and the perfume are different and far less familiar to most drinkers.

The craft is about timing. The flowers go from plant to tea within a day: picked in the early morning, trimmed and cooled, then laid in with finished green tea so the leaf drinks up their scent. Makers sum it up as same-day flower, same-day scenting.

Expect a soft green tea under a sweet floral fragrance. Little is written about how it changes across steeps; like other scented greens it gives its perfume most freely at the start, so keep the lid on and do not overheat the water.

When buying, smell it first: a clean floral scent over real tea is what you want, not a perfume sitting on top of tired leaf. Look for the Shexian name on the bag if you want the local tea, because zhulan scenting is also a general category of scented tea in China.
history:
Zhulan is one of the recognised flowers of Chinese scented tea, alongside jasmine, magnolia and osmanthus, and far smaller in output than jasmine. Local reporting says the same-day scenting practice in Shexian has been handed down for several hundred years, but the origin, the dynasty and any early written record are poorly documented.

Today Shexian zhulan tea has a geographical indication covering the whole county, and its making is listed as intangible heritage with named inheritors.
